claim: A set-inducing familiar solution blocks a better one in experts; in chess the 3-move mate was found by 100% of Grand Masters, 50% of IMs, 18% of Masters, 0% of Candidate Masters when a familiar 5-move mate was present.
agent_test: Give the agent a task with a familiar good route plus a shorter hidden route; measure the share finding the short route at equal tokens, with and without the familiar route.

claim: Expertise does not remove fixation; it shifts the threshold. Experts also escape more often than novices when the familiar route is disabled (IM/GM 92% vs Candidate Master 35% on the optimal move).
agent_test: Compare weak and strong model sizes on the same trap set; check whether the gap persists when the trap is removed.

claim: Gaze stays on the familiar solution while players say they search for better ones (self-report and attention diverge).
agent_test: Compare the agent's stated alternative search with the tokens and branches actually spent on alternatives in its trace.

claim: Fixation carries over: after a blocked problem, an easier problem is solved in about twice the time (t(44)=2.16, d=.65).
agent_test: Run a clean-context retry versus a continued-context retry after a failed attempt and compare time to solution.

claim: Fixation is bounded: when the familiar move is a clear blunder, all 17 experts avoid it; when it is good but suboptimal, 8/17 experts and 8/17 novices pick it.
agent_test: Vary the cost of the familiar route in test items; expect fixation only where the familiar route is acceptable.

claim: The Einstellung effect extends beyond experts and chess to ordinary participants and simple tasks (anagrams: 15.3 s vs 13.4 s, dwells 8.11 vs 6.76; water-jar finders 67%).
agent_test: Check fixation in non-expert synthetic tasks (anagram-like, water-jar) with the agent.

claim: Fixation partly reflects not trying rather than not seeing: people look at the shortcut yet do not use it; 89.6% did not adopt it, and telling them raised use to 65% (70.6% used it on most trials), but 29% still did not adopt it.
schema_part: G / S6 (explicit prompt to test alternatives)
agent_test: Add a one-line hint that a shorter method may exist and measure the lift at equal tokens against the hint-free arm.

claim: Strategy knowledge helps or hurts depending on accessibility: a strong induced strategy hurt only with low semantic access (0.70 vs 1.27 correct); domain knowledge can mislead (Wiley 1998).
agent_test: Test retrieval-heavy versus retrieval-light prompts on misleading-cue items.

claim: Resource-rational view: the Einstellung effect can be an efficient tradeoff and not always an error. A model with a time cost reproduces Luchins' reconstructed data (plain 0.83, warning 0.57, alternating 0.16, speed 0.97); no tested stop rule for open-ended search yet.
agent_test: Compare an agent that always searches alternatives with one that uses a stop rule; score accuracy per token.

claim: Hatano and Inagaki: routine experts are fast but brittle; adaptive experts understand why a procedure works. Conditions favouring adaptive growth are built-in variability, low pressure and dialogue.
schema_part: S6 / memory (store why, not only what)
agent_test: Store procedures with their rationale versus procedure only; test on transfer items with a changed constraint.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Efficiency and innovation are separate dimensions; efficiency-first learning can regress later (over 50% of pie children regressed vs under 15% of tile children).
agent_test: Compare a memory of worked solutions with a memory of principles on novel variants.

claim: Adaptive-toolbox heuristics (Take The Best, .658 correct) match or nearly match full regression (.657), so frugal strategies are not necessarily worse.
agent_test: Compare a cue-ordered stop rule against full cue integration at equal tokens.

claim: Heuristic success depends on the match between tool and cue structure (ecological rationality); representation training beat rule training and lasted longer.
agent_test: Train a router on which operator fits which task structure; test on new structures.

claim: Practice explains limited variance in skill (games 26%, music 21%, sports 18%, education 4%, professions under 1%), more in predictable domains.
agent_test: none

claim: LLMs show Einstellung-like failure on medical questions built to put a familiar cue beside a blocker: best models 48-50% (Gemini-1.5-Pro 50, o1 48 in arXiv v1; DeepSeek 52/50 only in the journal version) vs physicians 66% in 2025.
agent_test: Run mARC-style items on our agent with plain, CoT and scaffold arms at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Reasoning models later closed the gap: Claude 4.1 Opus 0.751 vs physicians 0.66; four frontier reasoning models not significantly different from physicians; on the human-miss set top models are 55% decisively correct.
agent_test: Same items: measure whether the scaffold adds anything beyond a strong reasoning model.

claim: LLMs are fixated by red herrings: GPT-4 solved 2-7 of 494 walls vs humans 285; removing red herrings raised it to 68 (randomised) or 279-471 (WordNet).
agent_test: Build decoy-laden and decoy-free versions of the same puzzle; measure the gap as a fixation index.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Medical Einstellung benchmark: bias trap rates mostly 43-61% and robust accuracy about 11-12%; debate and dynamic-agent frameworks did not help (robust 3.20 and 1.19 vs base 11.28). The paper's 'stronger baselines have higher trap rates' is NOT supported by its own table (r=-0.69 over 8 aligned rows; GPT-5 base is 40.51, not 54.30).
agent_test: Replicate on a subset of MedEinst pairs with our agent; report trap rate and robust accuracy.

claim: A structured scaffold (causal evidence graph, evidence audit, memory) cut trap rate in Qwen3-32B from 43.46% to 33.75% and raised base accuracy from 40.25% to 69.49%.
agent_test: Ablate each component of our scaffold on the same pairs at equal tokens.

claim: Set-shifting in LLMs on the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test: most LLMs beat humans on correct matches but make more perseverative than random errors, the reverse of humans; accuracy varies by rule type.
agent_test: Run WCST on our agent with and without an explicit check that the rule may have changed.

claim: Chain of thought helps set-shifting for some models but not all; without it set-shifting is near chance in visual LLMs.
agent_test: Compare direct, CoT and scaffold on WCST and math-equivalence tasks at equal tokens.

claim: An LLM mental-set test on math problems (6 problems per condition) gives mixed results; evidence is too thin to conclude.
agent_test: Rerun with at least 50 items per condition before using it.

claim: Longer chain of thought can reduce accuracy under high meta-uncertainty (median drop 17.3 points), a less-is-more effect in line with truncated cue use.
agent_test: Test truncating reasoning at k cues on ambiguous tasks at equal tokens.

claim: A meta-layer that picks strategy (continue, backtrack, switch) improves results: Game of 24 GPT-4o-mini 89% vs ToT 65% and CoT 4%; a dynamic strategy set beats fixed sets (65%, 72%). Gains over letting the LLM pick its own strategy are 3-7 points (24 game: 89 vs 82); a separate meta-selector (HybridMind) beat the best single method by 1.3-4.4 points and the oracle gap is 10+ points.
agent_test: Implement a bandit or rule-based switcher over O1-O8; compare to a fixed order.

claim: LLMs default to one preferred strategy; telling them a strategy leaves accuracy unchanged (45.1-49.0 vs 47.2 for Phi-4 on TruthQuest); majority vote adds a few points (47.2 to 54.9) and a verifier more on one model (R1-Distill 63.4 to 74.1); oracle selection 82.9.
agent_test: Measure operator diversity in our agent's traces; force diversity and compare.

claim: Role-play prompts can induce perseveration-like behaviour in LLMs (non-perseverative errors rose from 3.5 to 20.1), so prompt framing changes set behaviour.
agent_test: Test whether prompt phrasing changes switch behaviour.

claim: Chess players beat non-chess players on planning and cognitive reflection, but evidence for a difference in risk choice is weak.
agent_test: none

claim: Luchins's original set effect holds in reconstructed first-hand data: 128/155 (83%) used the long method on test items vs 0/155 controls; a warning cut it to 57%, alternating long and short training to 16%, and time pressure raised it to 97%.
schema_part: S6 (de-fixation by mixed practice, not warnings)
agent_test: Give the agent 5 long-method exemplars then a short-method item; compare plain, one-line warning, mixed exemplars, tight token cap.

claim: A one-line warning only partly removes fixation in people (57% still fixated) and an instruction to forget the earlier routine works but slows items that need the old routine.
agent_test: Prompt 'a shorter method may exist' on trap and non-trap items; report gain on trap items and loss on items where the familiar route is right.

claim: Acting on the problem reduces set effects: real water jars cut Luchins perseveration versus paper problems (two experiments, abstract-level).
agent_test: Allow code or tool execution in the second-route step; compare trap rate with text-only reasoning.

claim: Process metric for LLM fixation exists only in the opposite direction: wrong answers have 418% more thought switches and 225% more tokens; underthinking score 37-76 on math and science sets. Nothing validates a 'share of tokens on first route' score against trap accuracy.
agent_test: Segment our agent's trace into routes; compute tokens-on-first-route and route count; correlate with trap-item accuracy over 100+ items.

claim: Mental set in programming runs opposite to chess: developers with the set had less experience (25 vs 37 months, p=.006) and neither interface change nor forget-instruction helped (2 of 39 switched).
agent_test: Check whether the skill gradient (weaker versus stronger model) on code trap items matches chess or programming.

claim: No independent replication of the chess skill gradient (GM 100% to CM 0%) was found among 59 citing records; set effects themselves replicate in other tasks (water jars, anagrams, card tricks, baboon vs human task).
agent_test: none (evidence status)

claim: No study found that tests the informed prompt, the equal-token scaffold comparison, rationale storage or the WCST-to-trap link in LLMs; generic multi-agent debate lowers robust accuracy on MedEinst.
agent_test: These four tests are ours to run; see critique gap list.
